bib.title: "Why Should I Trust You?": Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Why Should I Trust You?" Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier. Ribeiro, Singh, Guestrin. KDD 2016 (arXiv:1602.04938v3).

COVERAGE: 59,435 of 59,435 chars, all 10 pages. References skimmed for origins. I also rendered p8 to check Figure 9. Nothing was skipped.

CLAIMS
(Quotes are verbatim, with line breaks and end-of-line hyphens collapsed. "where" gives the page and char offset.)

- claim: A snow-trained bad classifier fooled some subjects until they saw explanations; trust fell and snow identification rose.
  number: trusted 10/27 to 3/27; snow 12/27 to 25/27
  setup: Logistic regression on Inception first max-pool features. 20 hand-selected training images (all wolves with snow, huskies without). Subjects were graduate students with at least one graduate ML course. They saw 10 test predictions (8 correct), before then after explanations. 3 evaluators judged answers by majority. Authors concede a small sample.
  quote: "Trusted the bad model 10 out of 27 3 out of 27 / Snow as a potential feature 12 out of 27 25 out of 27"; "Although our sample size is small"
  where: p9, 46081, 47532

- claim: The classifier's snow behaviour is the observed result on extra images, and it also keys on light background.
  number: 20 training, 60 additional images
  setup: Same model, trained badly on purpose.
  quote: "We train a logistic regression classiﬁer on a training set of 20 images"; "On a collection of additional 60 images, the classiﬁer predicts “Wolf” if there is snow (or light background at the bottom), and “Husky” otherwise"
  where: p8, 44945, 45223

- claim: Non-experts choosing between two classifiers did best with SP-LIME, and all methods beat the test-accuracy choice, which picks the wrong model.
  number: correct choice: greedy RP 68.0, greedy SP 80.0, LIME RP 75.0, LIME SP 89.0 (%)
  setup: MTurk, 100 users per setting, K=6 and B=6. SVM RBF on 20 newsgroups Christianity/Atheism, original vs cleaned.
  quote: "68.0 75.0 80.0 89.0" (bar values; mapping read from the rendered figure, see PROBLEMS); "we repeat the experiment with 100 users"
  where: p8, ~40000, 41110

- claim: Held-out accuracy ranks the two classifiers the wrong way round compared with a real-world proxy.
  number: test 94.0 vs 88.6; religion set 57.3 vs 69.0
  setup: The religion set is 819 webpages per class, built by the authors from DMOZ and curated lists.
  quote: "The original classiﬁer achieves an accuracy score of 57.3% on the religion dataset , while the “cleaned” classiﬁer achieves a score of 69.0%. In contrast, the test accuracy on the original 20 newsgroups split is 94.0% and 88.6%"
  where: p7, 39270

- claim: LIME recovers the known important features of interpretable models.
  number: >90% recall; 92.1/97.0 books, 90.2/97.8 DVDs (sparse LR/DT)
  setup: Sentiment on books and DVDs, 2000 reviews each (1600/400 split). Models limited to 10 features per instance, K=10, N=15,000. Baselines on books: parzen 72.8/78.9, greedy 64.3/37.0, random 17.4/20.6. On DVDs: parzen 60.8/80.6, greedy 63.4/47.6, random 19.2/17.4.
  quote: "LIME consistently provides > 90% recall for both classiﬁers on both datasets"
  where: p6, 32170

- claim: LIME's simulated trust judgements best match an oracle.
  number: F1 91.8 to 96.7 for LIME; parzen 81.7 to 94.3; greedy 45.0 to 58.1; random 14.2 to 14.8
  setup: 25% of features randomly declared untrustworthy (artificial, as authors note). LR, NN, RF and SVM on books and DVDs, 100 runs.
  quote: "LIME 96.6 94.5 96.2 96.7 96.6 91.8 96.1 95.6"; "all results are signiﬁcant at p = 0.01"
  where: p7, 33567 onward

- claim: Crowd workers improved a classifier by deleting words, without ML knowledge or sight of the evaluation set.
  number: 3.6 min per round; just under 11 min total; 200 (SP) vs 157 (RP) words removed; 174 of 200 chosen by at least half, 68 by all
  setup: B=10, K=10. 10 subjects, then 5 per classifier per round, giving 250 classifiers after 3 rounds. Figure 10 gives accuracies only as a chart.
  quote: "Each subject took an average of 3.6 minutes per round of cleaning, resulting in just under 11 minutes"; "out of an average of 200 words selected with SP, 174 were selected by at least half of the users, while 68 by all the users"
  where: p8, 43736, 44101

- claim: Explanations exposed a spurious feature behind a high-accuracy model.
  number: 94% accuracy; "Posting" in 22% of training examples, 99% of those Atheism
  setup: RBF SVM on unigrams.
  quote: "achieves 94% held-out accuracy"; "The word “Posting” appears in 22% of examples in the training set, 99% of them in the class “Atheism”"
  where: p4, 21721, 22008

- claim: Explanation cost depends on the model's prediction time and N, not dataset size.
  number: under 3 s (RF, 1000 trees, N=5000); about 10 min (Inception per prediction)
  setup: Laptop, no GPU or parallelization, for the RF case.
  quote: "explaining random forests with 1000 trees using scikit-learn (http://scikit-learn.org) on a laptop with N = 5000 takes under 3 seconds"; "takes around 10 minutes"
  where: p4, 19893, 20064

- claim: Submodular pick has a greedy approximation guarantee for an NP-hard coverage problem.
  number: 1−1/e
  setup: Weighted coverage over the explanation matrix. The importance function is only defined for text.
  quote: "a constant-factor approximation guarantee of 1−1/e to the optimum"
  where: p6, 28294

- claim: SP-LIME best identified the better model in simulation.
  number: 800 runs; pairs within 0.1% validation, at least 5% test difference
  setup: Random forests with 30 trees, 10 artificial noisy features.
  quote: "until their validation accuracy is within 0.1% of each other, but their test accuracy diﬀers by at least 5%"; "averaged over 800 runs"
  where: p7, 35778, ~36700

- claim (method, no number): LIME minimises L(f,g,πx)+Ω(g). It samples by switching off interpretable components, weights samples by an exponential proximity kernel (cosine for text, L2 for images), selects K features with Lasso, then fits by least squares.
  where: p3 to p4

LIMITS
- Text and images only. "tabular", "categorical" and "numeric" have 0 hits; the flu figure is an illustration, not an experiment.
- Conceded: "if the underlying model is highly non-linear even in the locality of the prediction, there may not be a faithful explanation" (p4, 20539). Some behaviours fall outside the representation, e.g. sepia-toned images read as retro.
- Conceded: local fidelity does not imply global fidelity (p3, 12313).
- Left as future work: varying K; the pick step for images; other explanation families; "theoretical properties (such as the appropriate number of samples)" (p10).
- "fairly robust to sampling noise" (p3, 17415) is asserted, not measured. Stability across seeds is never tested ("stabil" and "seed" have 0 hits).
- My reading of the design, not the authors' concession:
  - Husky vs Wolf is a same-subject before/after with fixed order, no control group and no significance test.
  - Fidelity is tested only on models already interpretable.
  - The trust oracle uses randomly assigned bad features.
  - The religion set is an authors' proxy for "real world".
- Dated: no SHAP comparison (predates it); 2016 hardware timings.

BUILDS ON
- Baehrens et al. 2010 (parzen/gradient explanation).
- Strumbelj and Kononenko 2010 (perturbing inputs).
- Craven and Shavlik 1996, Sanchez et al. 2015 (surrogates).
- Efron et al. 2004 (regularization path).
- Krause and Golovin 2014, Feige 1998 (submodularity and hardness).
- Martens and Provost 2014 (greedy baseline).
- Kaufman et al. 2011 (leakage).
- Blitzer et al. 2007 (sentiment data).
- Szegedy et al. 2015 (Inception).
- Mikolov et al. 2013 (word2vec).

CODE: Algorithm 1 (p4): "w← K-Lasso(Z,K ) ⊿ with z′i as features, f(z) as target". Replication link: https://github.com/marcotcr/lime-experiments (p6, not visited).

FIGURES
- Fig 3, p4, "Toy example to present intuition for LIME": shows local sampling, proximity weights and a locally but not globally faithful line at once.
- Fig 11, p9, "Raw data and explanation of a bad model's prediction in the 'Husky vs Wolf' task": the snow explanation is instantly visible. Caption only; I did not view it.
- Fig 2, p2, competing classifiers for Christianity vs Atheism: shows the higher-accuracy model using junk words.
- Fig 10, p8, feature engineering across rounds: shows gains against the no-cleaning baseline, but prints no values.
- Fig 9, p8: human model choice by explainer and pick.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction order is misleading for Figure 9: "68.0 75.0 80.0 89.0" reads across the chart wrongly. The rendered page shows greedy 68/80 and LIME 75/89. Do not map these from text order.
- Fig 9's legend misprints "Submodular Pick (RP)"; it should be SP.
- Fig 10 values are not quotable, so I left them out.
- No embedded instructions.

COMPARISON WITH THE NOTES
Verdict: I found no flatly wrong figure or fact. The issues are under-qualification and a few statements this paper does not support. Citation rows in both references.md files are accurate, and the PDF path exists.

data-science/01-classical-ml/notes/08-model-interpretability.md

1. Line 271, the result is missing. The note says the experiment "tests whether subjects can detect that" and stops. Missing: 27 graduate students with ML coursework; trust 10/27 to 3/27; snow 12/27 to 25/27; authors' concession "our sample size is small"; no control group.
2. Line 271, under-qualified classifier claim. "said 'wolf' whenever there was snow" holds on the 60 additional images, and the paper adds "(or light background at the bottom)". The note also omits that huskies were selected without snow, and that the 20 images were hand selected.
3. Line 271, "copies of the row" imports a tabular framing the paper never tests. Its perturbation runs over binary interpretable components (words, super-pixels), and all experiments are text or images. Applying it to tabular rows is an extension beyond this source.
4. Line 271, method is incomplete. It omits proximity weighting and the K-feature limit, which are the parts that make it local and small.
5. Line 271, "best-known demonstration" is not supported by this paper and is unverifiable from it. The paper's larger human studies are the 100-per-setting model choice (89%) and the feature engineering study.
6. Line 57, "Depends on the sampling", differs from the paper's own unmeasured "fairly robust to sampling noise". The note's caution may be justified, but not by this source; if kept, it needs another citation or should be stated as the note's own view.
7. Line 328, "heuristic weights": the paper specifies an exponential kernel with width σ, tuned by cross-validation in §5.1, with no derivation. The characterisation is compatible but comes from the comparison with SHAP, not from this paper.

data-science/03-nlp/notes/06-sentiment-analysis.md

1. Line 299, "LIME earns its cost on nonlinear models" is unqualified. The paper warns that a model highly non-linear in the locality may have no faithful explanation. The paper gives no cost figures in this sentence's terms; its numbers are under 3 s (RF, N=5000) and about 10 min (Inception).
2. Line 299, "the global coefficients already explain the model" is the note's stance, and the paper partly cuts against it. It says a linear model may not be interpretable if "hundreds or thousands of features" contribute, and that globally important features may not matter locally. The paper also runs LIME on LR. This matters here because the note's example is TF-IDF plus LR.
3. Line 299, "more principled" SHAP is not supported by this paper, which has no SHAP comparison. The Ribeiro citation only points onward, so this is not a misattribution, but the reader needs Lundberg and Lee for it.
4. Lines 280 and 289, setup gap. `num_samples=1000` and `num_features=8` sit below or apart from anything in the paper: N=5000 (timing), N=15,000 (experiments), K=10 or K=6. The paper leaves the right sample count open. Worth a line, and it supports the seed warning at line 392, though the paper itself never measures stability.
5. Line 280, "you need a model with `predict_proba`" is an API fact, not a method requirement: the paper allows "the probability (or a binary indicator)" (p3, 15457). I did not check the library's behaviour.
6. Line 280 is otherwise accurate on dropping words and fitting a local linear model, but it omits proximity weighting and has no citation of its own; the citation appears 19 lines later.
7. Available but unused: the paper's simulated experiments are themselves sentiment tasks (books and DVD reviews), so the >90% recall and F1 results come with a directly relevant setup.

Lines 392 and 472 of the NLP note are consistent with the paper.
